newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Out-of-the-money puts dominate short stg.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Out-of-the-money puts dominate short stg.

text.p: Out-of-the-money puts stole the limelight in otherwise quiet trade in short sterling options on LIFFE on Thursday, as bullish sentiment pervaded the market, traders said.
However, there was only a slight movement in implied volatility as it remained locked at low levels, but unable to break down much further, they added.

"Bullish selling of September puts has been the main feature of trade today," said a trader at a French brokerage in London. "There seems to be optimism about sterling, and there are no real worries about an incoming Labour government."

Traders said the low level of volatility -- despite the fact that the ruling Conservative government must call a general election in the next three months -- suggests that the market has few worries about the opposition Labour Party reviving its old "tax and spend" reputation.
Implied volatility of short sterling options rose to more than 50 percent before the last election in 1992, when a Labour victory was also mooted.

March options on March futures were trading at a volatility of 6.0 percent, little changed from Wednesday, but traders said the proximity of the options and futures expiry on March 19 meant the level had little relevance.
June at-the-money volatility was hovering either side of 10 percent, a level which has proved to be the pivot point for the market since mid-January.
September volatility ticked down to 11.65 percent, from 12.00 percent earlier in the day, while December was down slightly at 13.0 percent from 13.1 percent.
June short sterling futures were up 0.05 at 93.58, while September was up 0.07 at 93.37 and December was up 0.07 at 93.22.
A trader at a Japanese bank said volatility was expected to tick lower, following a slide in Euromark volatility as well.
The French bank trader however, said the historic cheapness of short sterling volatility meant it was hard to push further down.
"It can only go down another one percentage point," he said.
September puts were the most active. By 1200 GMT, 3,100 contracts had been traded at the 93.00 strike and 1,100 at the 93.25 strike.
In December, 300 contracts were traded at the 93.00 strike and 200 at 93.25.
In contrast, call activity was generally limited. The most notable trades were 400 September calls at 93.00, 300 December calls at 93.00 and 600 at at 93.25.
